blocks.text: Write the outgoing message to a table in the same transaction as the data, then publish it from there reliably.

Updating a database and publishing to a broker cannot share one atomic transaction (the dual-write problem). With an **outbox**, the message becomes a row in the same database commit as the business change. A separate **relay** reads unsent rows, publishes them, and marks them sent.

items: **Atomic:** the state change and its event commit or roll back together.
**Relay:** a poller or change-data-capture tails the outbox.

blocks.text: The outbox fixes lost and phantom events, not duplicates. A relay crash between publish and mark re-sends the row.

walkthrough.note: A transaction buffers both the order and its outbox row. Commit writes them together; any exception drops both, so a rolled-back order never leaves a message behind.
The relay scans unpublished rows. It marks a row published only after the broker acknowledges, so a failure keeps the row for the next poll.
The first transaction commits an order and its row. The second throws before commit: no order, no outbox row, and the sequence gap is harmless.
A scripted broker fails on its first call. Poll 1 sends nothing, poll 2 delivers the row, poll 3 finds nothing left. Delivery happened exactly once here, but could repeat after a crash.

blocks.text: Announcing a new booking to downstream systems.

A booking service inserts a reservation and must tell billing, email and analytics. Publishing to Kafka after the commit loses the event if the process dies in between; publishing before the commit announces bookings that roll back. The service inserts a `booking_created` row into an `outbox` table inside the transaction, and Debezium streams that table's inserts to Kafka.

blocks.text: Payoff: no booking exists without its event, and no event exists without its booking, even across crashes and broker outages.

lists.title: Use when
items: A state change must be followed by an event, without losing or inventing either.
Distributed transactions across database and broker are unavailable or too costly.
Other services depend on your events for their own consistency.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The event is purely best-effort telemetry where loss is acceptable.
The database is also your broker, such as event sourcing, where the log is already the outbox.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Duplicates after relay crashes: consumers need ids and deduplication.
Outbox growth: purge or archive sent rows, or the table degrades.
Ordering: polling by id can reorder across concurrent transactions; key per aggregate.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Outbox rows that carry full database snapshots instead of intent-level events.
Polling every 50 ms where change-data-capture would remove the load.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records model outbox rows well; serialize payloads with Jackson into a JSON column.
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets several relays poll without claiming the same rows.

rows.difference: The outbox guarantees at-least-once publication. The idempotent consumer on the other side makes the redelivered duplicates harmless.
A saga needs each local step and its message to be atomic. Each participant uses an outbox to publish its commands and events safely.
Domain events describe what happened inside a model. The outbox is the delivery mechanism that gets them out of the service reliably.
A unit of work batches changes into one commit. The outbox adds a message row to that same commit and a relay that publishes it.
With event sourcing the event log is the source of truth, so publishing from it replaces a separate outbox table.

entries.name: Outbox Event Router
entries.detail: An SMT (`io.debezium.transforms.outbox.EventRouter`) turns inserts into the outbox table into Kafka messages routed by aggregate type.

entries.name: Event publication registry
entries.detail: Persists event publications in the same transaction and republishes incomplete ones, giving an outbox for application events.

entries.name: Message table
entries.detail: Writes messages to a `message` table inside the business transaction and relays them to Kafka via CDC or polling.

entries.name: Outbox extension
entries.detail: Firing a CDI `ExportedEvent` writes an outbox row in the current transaction; Debezium's `EventRouter` then streams it to Kafka.

options.why: Store the event in the same commit as the payment and let a relay publish it, so a crash cannot drop it.
Retries run in the process; if the process dies between commit and publish there is nothing left to retry.
Breakers protect against a failing dependency but cannot recover an event lost with a dead process.

exercises.prompt: Explain the Transactional Outbox: the problem it solves, how it works, and what guarantee it gives.

modelAnswer.text: Writing to a database and publishing to a broker can't be atomic, so a crash can lose or invent events. The outbox stores the message in the same transaction as the data; a relay later publishes unsent rows and marks them sent. It gives at-least-once delivery, so consumers must deduplicate.

keyPoints: Dual-write problem: database and broker can't commit atomically
Message saved as a row in the business transaction
Relay publishes then marks the row, by polling or CDC
At-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible
